what: Learning from Black-Box Models by Maximum Interpretation Decomposition
title: Learning from Black-Box Models by Maximum Interpretation Decomposition
text: goal ‘midr’ provide model-agnostic method interpreting explaining black-box predictive models creating globally interpretable surrogate model. package implements ‘Maximum Interpretation Decomposition’ (MID), functional decomposition technique finds optimal additive approximation original model. approximation achieved minimizing squared error predictions black-box model surrogate model. theoretical foundations MID described Iwasawa & Matsumori (2026) [Forthcoming], package detailed Asashiba et al. (2025).

title: Learning from Black-Box Models by Maximum Interpretation Decomposition
text: following example, fit random forest model Boston dataset included ISLR2, attempt interpret using functions midr. first step create MID model global surrogate target model using interpret(). visualize main interaction effects variables, apply ggmid() plot() fitted MID model.   mid.importance() helps compute compare importance main interaction effects.  mid.breakdown() provides way analyze individual predictions decomposing differences intercept predicted value variable effects.  mid.conditional() can used compute ICE curves (Goldstein et al. 2015) fitted MID model, well breakdown ICE curves main interaction effects.
code: # load required packages library(midr) library(ggplot2) library(gridExtra) library(ISLR2) library(ranger) theme_set(theme_midr("xy")) # split the Boston dataset data("Boston", package = "ISLR2") set.seed(42) idx <- sample(nrow(Boston), nrow(Boston) * .75) train <- Boston[ idx, ] valid <- Boston[-idx, ] # fit a random forest model rf <- ranger(medv ~ ., train, mtry = 5) preds_rf <- predict(rf, valid)$predictions cat("RMSE: ", weighted.loss(valid$medv, preds_rf)) #> RMSE:  3.351362 # fit a two-dimensional MID model mid <- interpret(medv ~ .^2, train, rf, lambda = .1) mid #>  #> Call: #> interpret(formula = medv ~ .^2, data = train, model = rf, lambda = 0.1) #>  #> Model Class: ranger #>  #> Intercept: 22.446 #>  #> Main Effects: #> 12 main effect terms #>  #> Interactions: #> 66 interaction terms #>  #> Uninterpreted Variation Ratio: 0.016248 preds_mid <- predict(mid, valid) cat("RMSE: ", weighted.loss(preds_rf, preds_mid)) #> RMSE:  1.106667 cat("RMSE: ", weighted.loss(valid$medv, preds_mid)) #> RMSE:  3.306324 # visualize the main and interaction effects of the MID model grid.arrange(   ggmid(mid, "lstat") +     labs(title = "Feature Effects",          subtitle = "Main Effect of 'lstat'"),   ggmid(mid, "dis") +     labs(title = "", subtitle = "Main effect of 'dis'"),   ggmid(mid, "lstat:dis") +     labs(subtitle = "Interaction Effect of 'lstat:dis'"),   ggmid(mid, "lstat:dis", main.effects = TRUE, type = "compound") +     labs(subtitle = "Total Effect of 'lstat:dis'") ) # visualize all main effects grid.arrange(grobs = mid.plots(mid), nrow = 3) # visualize the MID importance of the component functions imp <- mid.importance(mid) grid.arrange(nrow = 1L,   ggmid(imp, fill = "steelblue", max.nterms = 20) +     theme(legend.position = "none") +     labs(title = "Feature Effect Importance",          subtitle = "Bar Plot"),   ggmid(imp, "heatmap", linewidth=.25, color="gray85") +     theme(legend.position = "none") +     labs(title = "", subtitle = "Heat Map") ) # visualize the MID breakdown of the model predictions bd1 <- mid.breakdown(mid, data = train, row = 1L) bd9 <- mid.breakdown(mid, data = train, row = 9L) grid.arrange(nrow = 1L,   ggmid(bd1, fill = "steelblue") +     theme(legend.position = "none") +     labs(title = "Additive Breakdown of Predictions",          subtitle = "Waterfall Plot for Row 1"),   ggmid(bd9, theme = "shap", size = 3, type = "dotchart") +     theme(legend.position = "none") +     labs(title = "", subtitle = "Dot Chart for Row 9") ) # visualize the ICE curves of the MID model ice <- mid.conditional(mid, "lstat", max.nsamples = 100) grid.arrange(   ggmid(ice, color = "steelblue") +     labs(title = "Individual Conditional Expectation",          subtitle = "ICE Plot of 'lstat'"),   ggmid(ice, "centered", color = "steelblue") +     labs(title = "", subtitle = "c-ICE Plot of 'lstat'"),   ggmid(ice, term = "lstat:dis", var.color = dis) +     labs(subtitle = "Interaction Effect with 'dis'"),   ggmid(ice, term = "lstat:age", var.color = age) +     labs(subtitle = "Interaction Effect with 'age'") )

title: Fit MID Models — interpret
text: Maximum Interpretation Decomposition (MID) functional decomposition framework designed serve faithful surrogate complex, black-box models. deconstructs target prediction function \(f(\mathbf{X})\) set highly interpretable components: $$f(\mathbf{X}) = g_\emptyset + \sum_{j} g_j(X_j) + \sum_{j<k} g_{jk}(X_j, X_k) + g_D(\mathbf{X})$$ \(g_\emptyset\) intercept, \(g_j(X_j)\) represents main effect feature \(j\), \(g_{jk}(X_j, X_k)\) represents second-order interaction features \(j\) \(k\), \(g_D(\mathbf{X})\) residual. components \(g_j\) \(g_{jk}\) modeled linear expansion basis functions, resulting piecewise linear piecewise constant functions. estimation performed minimizing penalized squared residual objective representative dataset: $$\text{minimize } \mathbf{E}[g_D(\mathbf{X})^2] + \lambda R(g;\mathbf{X})$$ \(\lambda \ge 0\) regularization parameter controls smoothness components penalizing second-order differences adjacent coefficients (discrete roughness penalty). ensure uniqueness identifiability decomposition, MID imposes centering constraints: feature \(j\), \(\mathbf{E}[g_j(X_j)] = 0\); feature pair \((j, k)\), \(\mathbf{E}[g_{jk}(X_j, X_k) \mid X_j = x_j] = 0\) \(x_j\) \(\mathbf{E}[g_{jk}(X_j, X_k) \mid X_k = x_k] = 0\) \(x_k\). cases least-squares solution still unique due collinearity, additional probability-weighted minimum-norm constraint applied coefficients ensure stable unique solution.

"shifted.identity": shifted identity link \(\eta = \mu + h\) shift parameter h (default 1). "robit": robit link using Student's t-distribution CDF. \(\eta = F_{t}^{-1}(\mu, \nu)\) degrees freedom parameter df (alias nu, default 7). "asinh": inverse hyperbolic sine transformation \(\eta = \text{asinh}(\lambda \mu)\) scale parameter lambda (default 1). "scobit": skewed logit link \(\eta = \text{logit}(\mu^{1/\alpha})\). parameter alpha (default 1) controls asymmetry tails. alpha=1 corresponds standard logistic regression. "box-cox": Box-Cox transformation \(\eta = (\mu^\lambda - 1)/\lambda\) power parameter lambda (default 0). "box-cox2": two-parameter Box-Cox transformation \(\eta = ((\mu + \lambda_2)^{\lambda_1} - 1)/\lambda_1\) parameters lambda1 (power, default 0) lambda2 (shift, default 1). "yeo-johnson": Yeo-Johnson transformation parameter lambda (default 0). Handles negative values.

title: Extended Parametric Link Functions — make_link
code: # Standard Box-Cox with lambda = 0.5 (Square root-like) lk <- make_link("box-cox", lambda = 0.5) plot(x <- seq(1, 100, length.out = 50), lk$linkfun(x), type = "l")   # Yeo-Johnson with lambda = 1.5 (Handles negative values) lk <- make_link("yeo-johnson", lambda = 1.5) plot(x <- seq(-100, 100, length.out = 50), lk$linkfun(x), type = "l")   # Robit link with df=2 (Heavier tails than probit) lk <- make_link("robit", df = 2) print(lk) #> Link Function: robit(df = 2) #>  #> function (mu)  #> stats::qt(mu, df = df) #> <environment: 0x5d46a0706f98> plot(x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 50), lk$linkinv(x), type = "l") lk <- make_link("robit", df = 1) cat(lk$name) # cauchit #> cauchit points(x, lk$linkinv(x), type = "l", lty = 2L) lk <- make_link("robit", df = Inf) cat(lk$name) # probit #> probit points(x, lk$linkinv(x), type = "l", lty = 3L)   # Scobit link with alpha=0.5 (Skewed) lk <- make_link("scobit", alpha = 0.5) plot(x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 50), lk$linkinv(x), type = "l")   # Inverse Hyperbolic Sine (Alternative to log for zero-inflated data) lk <- make_link("asinh", lambda = 10) plot(x <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 50), lk$linkfun(x), type = "l") lk <- make_link("log1p") points(x, lk$linkfun(x), type = "l", lty = 2L)   # Shifted log simplifies to log1p when h=1 make_link("shifted.log", h = 1) # Returns link="log1p" #> Link Function: log1p #>  #> function (mu)  #> log1p(mu) #> <environment: 0x5d46a313a630>  # Box-Cox with lambda=1 simplifies to shifted identity make_link("box-cox", lambda = 1) #> Link Function: shifted.identity(h = -1) #>  #> function (mu)  #> mu + h #> <environment: 0x5d46a010d110>

text: Optimized fitting process: Enhanced space (time) complexity constructing large design matrices, especially datasets many observations. Memory-efficient estimation: Introduced save.memory option interpret(). Improved design matrix constraints: Replaced max.ncol argument max.nelements interpret() provide intuitive control memory consumption design matrix.

title: midr 0.5.3
text: Memory-free prediction engine: Re-implemented prediction logic avoid storing massive term effect matrices, significantly reducing memory usage interpret() predict.mid(). Flexible formatting: plot.mid.breakdown() ggmid.mid.breakdown() now support format.args enhanced label.format better visualization control. CRAN compatibility: Updated various internal functions ensure consistent behavior ‘stats’ package (especially stats::terms()) improved documentation clarity.

title: midr 0.5.2.904
text: Memory-efficient interpret(): model object longer stores massive fitted.matrix (term-wise decomposition fitted values). Optimized predict() engine: Re-implemented prediction logic using matrix-free approach. -demand Decomposition: Functions like mid.importance() now perform term-wise decomposition --fly using new optimized prediction engine. mid.importance() introduced new argument max.nkeeps (default: 10,000). importance scores calculated using full dataset maximum accuracy, function now optionally retains weighted random sample term-wise predictions. Standardized predict outputs: type = "terms", intercept now stored constant attribute returned matrix, aligning standard R conventions (e.g., predict.lm). Removed redundant fitted.matrix reference interpret.default prevent memory leaks estimation process.
